rows.l1_text: In recent years, many countries have begun to restrict the use of single-use plastic products through legislation, which is part of a global trend.
The goal of these environmental policies is to reduce plastic pollution and protect natural resources.
Different countries have adopted different regulatory methods.
Some countries ban supermarkets from providing plastic bags for free, and people need to pay to buy them, which can reduce the amount used.
Other countries completely ban certain plastic products, such as plastic straws and tableware.
Governments also tax companies that make plastic, encouraging them to switch to environmentally friendly materials.
In Europe, some countries have introduced a "plastic bottle deposit system."
When customers buy a drink they pay a little extra, and after returning the empty bottle they can get the deposit back.
This method has greatly increased the recycling rate of plastic bottles.
Some cities in Asia, meanwhile, have strengthened waste sorting management, stipulating that residents must put plastic waste out separately, or else they will be fined.
Although these measures sometimes bring inconvenience to life, in the long run they are beneficial to the environment.
Although countries' policies differ, their purpose is the same: to reduce plastic waste.
Scientists point out that plastic is very hard to break down in the natural environment and will harm marine life.
Therefore, more and more countries are joining this action.
Experts believe that effective regulation requires the joint efforts of governments, companies, and the public.
Only if everyone cooperates can the problem of plastic pollution truly be solved.
This global trend also reminds us that protecting the environment is everyone's responsibility.
In the future there may be stricter laws introduced, pushing society toward a more sustainable direction.

The recycling symbol is an important symbolic meaning of environmentalism.

The three arrows of this symbol represent the three steps of waste management: reduce use, reuse, and recycle.
The first arrow is reducing what is thrown away, the second is using old things again, and the third is turning garbage into new things.
Although the recycling systems of different countries differ, this symbol helps people understand the importance of protecting the environment.
Today, we can see this symbol on cardboard boxes, plastic bottles and metal cans.

Making compost at home is a very practical do-it-yourself project that can both reduce waste and provide good fertilizer for gardening.
Many people throw organic waste such as vegetable leaves, fruit peels and coffee grounds from the kitchen into the trash can, but in fact these can all become useful compost.
First, prepare a plastic box with a lid and put it on a balcony or in a corner of the yard.
A few small holes should be made in the bottom of the box to allow drainage and air flow.
Next, first spread a layer of dry leaves or torn-up paper in the box, and then add kitchen waste.
Each time after adding wet waste, cover it with a layer of dry material, which can reduce the smell and also help decomposition.
Do not put meat, oil or dairy products into the compost box, because they easily attract insects and are also hard to decompose.
Every one or two weeks, turn the compost with a shovel to let air in, so that the waste will decompose faster.
After about two months, the original waste will turn into something dark brown and like soil, and this is compost.
Mix it into the soil of flower pots or vegetable gardens, and the plants will grow better.
This process reflects the idea of sustainability, because we are recycling resources instead of treating them as waste.
Making compost yourself is not only environmentally friendly, but also lets people understand the cycles of nature better.
Even small actions can have a positive impact on the environment.

In the development picture of contemporary metropolises, urban green spaces and vertical farms have gone beyond their purely ecological functions and become strategic elements that reshape the economic geography.

Parks, community gardens, and even the greening systems of building facades and rooftops, traditionally regarded as "non-productive space", are being deeply embedded in the urban capital cycle through multiple value chains.

The market premium mechanism of high-end real estate projects is significantly driven by landscape resources, and residential units adjacent to or integrating high-quality green space often achieve a value increase of more than 20%, a phenomenon especially prominent in the core areas of first-tier cities where land is scarce.

Investors no longer evaluate only floor area and location, but incorporate the accessibility of "green capital" into core risk assessment models, pushing developers to regard ecological infrastructure as a key lever for improving asset liquidity.
At the same time, vertical farms, as an advanced form of urban agriculture, are reconstructing the spatiotemporal logic of food security.

Through multi-layer hydroponics, aeroponics and artificial intelligence environmental control technologies, such facilities can achieve, within a three-dimensional space of tens of thousands of square meters, an output efficiency equivalent to hundreds of hectares of traditional farmland, and supply fresh leafy vegetables and medicinal plants without interruption all year round.
The characteristic of their location being close to the end consumer greatly reduces logistics losses and the carbon footprint, forming a resilient alternative to fragile global supply chains.

When frequent extreme weather causes fluctuations in staple grain producing areas, distributed urban food production networks show a significant risk-hedging capacity, leading local governments to include such projects in the emergency planning of critical infrastructure.
From the macro perspective of urban planning, sustainability has shifted from a moral initiative to economic rationality.

Mixed-use development is being redefined: a commercial complex integrating a vertical farm is no longer merely a display of corporate social responsibility, but becomes a business strategy for attracting high-end tenants and increasing brand stickiness.

Through policy tools such as floor area ratio bonuses and tax reductions, governments guide private investment toward construction projects with ecological service functions, thereby reducing long-term public spending on sewage treatment, heat island mitigation and air pollution control.

This innovative financing model of public-private collaboration has given rise to new financial instruments such as "environmental benefit bonds", which securitize externality benefits such as incremental carbon sinks, energy savings and improved residents' health, opening up a quantifiable return path for sustainable investment.
A more profound impact lies in putting spatial justice back on the agenda.
When green space and localized food production become scarce resources, their distribution pattern is directly linked to social stratification.

Cutting-edge urban governance practices are trying, through legal mandates and incentive mechanisms, to ensure that low-income communities also enjoy technology-enabled agricultural facilities and high-quality green space, avoiding the entrenchment of ecological privilege.

Against this background, the city is no longer regarded as the opposite of nature, but, through technological innovation and institutional design, becomes a complex adaptive system in which sustainability, food sovereignty and economic vitality evolve together.
The foundation of real estate value is shifting from the simple possession of physical space to the dynamic capacity to contribute to ecosystem service flows and community well-being.

In the precise system of modern aeronautical engineering, aircraft design is in essence an artistic application of physical laws, and aerodynamic principles in particular occupy a central position within it.
When an aircraft travels through the atmosphere, the interaction between its wings and the airflow determines the basic feasibility of flight.

The core of this process lies in the mechanism of lift generation: the airflow over the upper surface of the wing speeds up because of the greater curvature, causing the pressure to drop; by comparison, the airflow over the lower surface moves more slowly and the pressure is relatively higher.
This pressure difference is perpendicular to the direction of the airflow and forms an upward net force, namely lift.
According to Bernoulli's theorem, an increase in fluid velocity is necessarily accompanied by a decrease in static pressure, which provides a classical physical explanation for lift.

However, relying only on Bernoulli's principle is not enough to fully describe complex real flow phenomena, so modern aerodynamics tends more toward a combined analysis incorporating Newton's third law: the wing deflects the airflow downward through the angle of attack, and the airflow in turn pushes the wing upward with an equal and opposite force, thereby producing lift.
During flight, lift is not the only force acting on the aircraft.

Coexisting with it is drag, which is the opposing force that air exerts on the aircraft's forward motion, and which can be subdivided into several types, such as pressure drag, friction drag and induced drag.

Pressure drag arises from the pressure imbalance between the front and rear of the aircraft, and is especially pronounced where the fuselage cross-section changes sharply; friction drag comes from the viscous shear between air molecules and the aircraft surface, and is greatly affected by surface roughness and the Reynolds number; and induced drag is a by-product of lift, caused by the local downwash induced by wingtip vortices, and its strength increases as lift increases.

To achieve efficient cruising, aeronautical engineers must make fine trade-offs in the aerodynamic configuration in order to maximize the lift-to-drag ratio, that is, the lift that can be produced per unit of drag, which is a key indicator of flight efficiency.
From the perspective of engineering implementation, aircraft design is a multidisciplinary coupled optimization game.

Advances in materials science have allowed composite materials to be widely used, which has not only reduced structural weight but also enhanced fatigue durability; the development of computational fluid dynamics, CFD, in turn enables engineers to simulate aerodynamic performance under extreme conditions in a virtual wind tunnel, thereby completing multiple rounds of iteration before prototype manufacturing.
In addition, active flow control technologies, such as boundary layer suction or synthetic jets, are being explored for adjusting flow separation in real time, further extending the flight envelope.

Behind these cutting-edge technologies is the in-depth solution of the Navier-Stokes equations, whose nonlinear nature makes turbulence modeling to this day a problem that the physics community has not fully conquered.
It is worth noting that even in modern airliners highly integrated with autopilot and artificial intelligence, the basic physical laws of aerodynamics still cannot be violated.
All the control actions performed by pilots or flight control systems, whether pitch, roll or yaw, ultimately come down to the precise regulation of aerodynamic moments.

The aerodynamic challenges that an aircraft faces in different flight phases, such as takeoff, cruise and landing, differ, requiring the wing shape, such as the extension of flaps and slats, to adapt dynamically.
From this it can be seen that aeronautical engineering is not only a collection of technologies, but also an externalized expression of humanity's deep understanding of the laws of nature.

Every smooth takeoff and landing is the result of strict adherence to the laws of physics, and also demonstrates the outstanding ability of engineering wisdom to achieve controllability in complex systems.

In the practical dimension of contemporary environmental ethics, the home composting system has become a microcosmic vehicle that makes the concept of urban sustainability concrete, not only reflecting individuals' active assumption of ecological responsibility, but also constituting an indispensable distributed node in the city's waste reduction strategy.

Through the localized cyclical conversion of organic waste, household-level resource reuse mechanisms effectively shorten the traditional waste treatment chain, thereby lowering the carbon footprint and strengthening ecological resilience at the community level.

This do-it-yourself ecological intervention is essentially a gentle reconstruction of the industrialized consumption model, and behind it lies a deep horticultural philosophy, namely that a non-predatory, symbiotic relationship should be established between humans and the land.
To achieve efficient and hygienic home composting, the first thing is to understand the biochemical balance between "green materials" and "brown materials".

Green materials are rich in nitrogen and include wet organic matter such as kitchen fruit peels, coffee grounds and fresh grass clippings; brown materials provide a carbon source and are dry residues such as dry leaves, shredded cardboard and sawdust.

The ideal ratio is about 1:2 by volume, and this carbon-to-nitrogen ratio can promote the succession from mesophilic to thermophilic microbial communities, so that the pile rises to 55–65°C within a few days, effectively inactivating pathogens and weed seeds.
Special attention must be paid to strictly excluding animal residues such as meat, fats and dairy products, because they easily cause anaerobic fermentation and breed odors and pests.
The choice of compost container must suit local conditions.

City apartments can use a sealed worm composting bin, using the gut microbes of red earthworms, Eisenia fetida, to efficiently break down finely chopped kitchen scraps, producing "black gold" rich in plant growth hormones, a concentrated humus liquid.

Those with a yard should build a tiered compost bin, using physical separation to achieve continuous processing of the different fermentation stages: the bottom layer is the primary decomposition zone, the middle layer is the maturation transition zone, and new material is continuously added to the top layer.
Regularly turning the pile to ensure oxygen penetration and prevent local anaerobic acidification is the key operation for maintaining the activity of the microbial community.
From the perspective of ecological engineering, home composting is in fact a low-entropy cycle model.

Traditional landfilling makes organic matter decompose under oxygen-free conditions, releasing methane, CH₄, a potent greenhouse gas, while aerobic composting converts it into stable humus and sequesters carbon within the soil matrix.

When this matured product is applied to a home gardening system, it not only improves soil aggregate structure and increases water and nutrient retention, but also rebuilds the positive feedback loop among plants, microorganisms and organic matter.

Studies show that in planting beds with long-term application of homemade compost, the microbial diversity index is more than 40% higher than in the control group, significantly enhancing plants' stress resistance.
Especially profound is that this daily practice contains a "cognitive transformation effect" in the sense of behavioral ecology.

When individuals personally experience the complete cycle of a banana peel turning into fertile soil, the boundary of their cognition of the concept of "waste" will undergo a fundamental shift: waste is no longer the end point of linear consumption, but an intermediary in circular metabolism.

This embodied cognition in turn catalyzes broader sustainable lifestyle choices, forming a chain reaction of behaviors from waste reduction to low-carbon travel and from organic consumption to energy saving.

Therefore, home composting is not only a technical operation, but also a ritual practice of constructing ecological subjectivity, reshaping the ethical contract between humans and nature within micro-level life politics.

The evolution of musical notation systems profoundly reflects the historical process of humanity's understanding of the order of sound.
Since ancient times, different civilizations have tried to capture fleeting sounds with visual symbols, but early notation methods were mostly suggestive rather than precise.

Ancient Greece used letters to mark pitch, Byzantium used symbols to indicate the direction of the melody, and Chinese gongchepu used characters to record relative pitch positions; none of these systems specified rhythmic details, and their performance relied on the tradition of oral and personal transmission.

The truly revolutionary turning point began with the development of neume notation in Western Europe at the end of the Middle Ages, when monks added symbols above sacred texts to indicate the rise and fall of notes, which eventually evolved into the four-line staff, whose foundation was laid by Guido of Arezzo in the 11th century.
This system achieved a spatial representation of pitch through the clear correspondence between lines and spaces, and provided a necessary condition for the systematization of music theory.
By the Renaissance, the five-line staff was gradually established as the standard, and with the introduction of bar lines, key signatures and time signatures, notation became increasingly precise.
This technical evolution not only allowed the complex texture of polyphonic music to be conveyed accurately, but also profoundly influenced composers' ways of thinking.
Once sound could be completely recorded, composition was no longer confined to the realm of improvised performance, but became an intellectual activity that could be refined and revised on paper.

In the Baroque era, the popularity of figured bass notation further reflected the maturity of the concept of functional harmony; and from the Classical to the Romantic period, notation increasingly tended toward comprehensive control, with dynamics, tempo and expression markings appearing densely, reflecting the central position of individual emotional expression in music.
Since the 20th century, traditional notation has faced multiple challenges.

Schoenberg's twelve-tone system forced theorists to reconstruct the logic of pitch organization, and serialism brought parameters such as rhythm, duration and dynamics all under control, giving rise to a highly mathematical notational language.

At the same time, avant-garde composers such as John Cage questioned the authority of traditional notation, and developed graphic scores, text scores and even the open structures of chance music, emphasizing the performer's right to re-create.

The rise of electronic music brought an entirely new dimension: technical means such as spectral analysis, waveform diagrams and algorithmically generated scores allowed notation to go beyond the visual paradigm of the staff and enter the realm of data-based expression.
Today, the development of notation presents a pattern of diverse coexistence.

The traditional five-line staff is still the globally used technical language, supporting symphony orchestras, opera productions and academic composition teaching; while in the field of experimental music, mixed-media notation and real-time interactive notation, such as visual instructions in the Max/MSP environment, are constantly expanding the boundaries.

It is worth noting that after artificial intelligence became involved in music composition, machine-generated scores often combine symbolic logic with probabilistic models, prompting new discussions about "readability" and "playability".

Viewed from a historical dimension, notation is not only the evolution of a technical tool, but also a mirror of changes in the concept of the nature of music; it has both shaped composers' ways of imagining and reconstructed the cultural coding of auditory experience.

The development of notation is essentially humanity's eternal effort to capture infinite sonic possibilities with a limited system of symbols, and its trajectory of evolution is precisely a profound testimony to the interactive symbiosis of music theory and practice.

The history of music is long, and musical notation is also slowly developing.
The earliest music had no fixed way of being written, and people learned by ear.
Later, composers needed to write their music down so that more people could play it.
So, different notation systems appeared.
In ancient times, some places used letters to represent pitch, and some used symbols.
These methods were simple, but could not accurately record rhythm and note length.
With the progress of music theory, notation became more refined.
An early form of staff notation appeared in medieval Europe.
At first there were only two lines, and later it became five lines, which could show the height of notes more clearly.
This notation was used by many composers, and also spread to other regions.
Although different places have different habits, the five-line staff slowly became the internationally common method.
In China, there were also notation methods of their own in ancient times, such as gongchi notation and jianzi notation.
They use Chinese characters or symbols to record fingering and note positions, and suit traditional instruments.
Although many people today learn Western five-line staff notation, these ancient methods are still valuable.
Studying them can help us understand the history of music.
Modern technology has also brought new ways of notation.
Some composers use graphic scores, drawing music as images.
Others use digital software to edit sound directly.
These new methods make musical creation freer.
Overall, the development of notation reflects humanity's constant pursuit of musical expression.
From simple symbols to complex systems, it has helped music cross time and space, and be understood and played by more people.
SaaS companies need to take data and algorithm compliance seriously.
When users use a service, they provide a lot of personal information.
Companies must clearly tell users how this data will be used.
For example, the system needs to state which data is used to improve the product and which may be shared with partners.
If users do not understand the explanation, they cannot make the right choice.
Therefore, the text should be simple and clear, and avoid words that are too technical.
In addition, how the algorithm works should also have a certain degree of transparency.
Although it is not necessary to disclose all technical details, the basic logic must be explained.
For example, a recommendation system makes suggestions based on the user's browsing history.
This way, users can understand why they see certain content.
If the system makes an important decision, such as automatically rejecting an application, the user should know the main reason and have a chance to appeal.
The source of the training data is also important.
Companies should ensure that the data is lawfully obtained and does not contain sensitive information, such as health records or ID numbers.
Regularly checking data quality can reduce erroneous results.
Employees need to receive training, understand the importance of privacy protection, and know the consequences of violating the rules.
Finally, businesses must establish clear policies and accept external oversight.
Third-party audits can help find vulnerabilities.
Publishing an annual transparency report can make the public trust the service more.
Overall, disclosing data practices and algorithm principles is not a burden, but a key step in building long-term trust.

People yawn when they are tired.
When yawning, the mouth opens very wide and takes in a lot of air.
This is a function of the body.
Scientists study this phenomenon, and this is called biology.
Yawning may be related to brain temperature.
When the brain is too hot, yawning can make it a little cooler.
Neurology is the science that studies the brain and nerves.
Neurology has found that when people see others yawn, they want to yawn too.
This is the contagiousness of yawning.
If you see a classmate yawn in the classroom, you may want to yawn right away too.
Animals do this too.
Yawning is not because of laziness, but because the body needs it.
We should listen to our bodies.
When sleepy, yawn, and then go to sleep.
